text.p: The dollar reversed sharply against the yen in Europe as news of a much larger-than-expected U.S. July trade gap put the gloss back on the yen and increased concern about a third-quarter economic slowdown.
Surging imports, including costlier foreign oil, sent the trade gap soaring 42.6 percent to $11.68 billion, its highest in more than eight years and the $8.8 billion gap expected.
The July trade deficit with Japan also widened sharply, up 32.9 percent to $4.31 billion, helping to put the yen back in the spotlight across the board.

"The large Japan trade gap is likely to neutralise the dollar uptrend against the yen, even though I would caution against reading too much into a monthly figure," said Joe Prendergast, FX strategist at Merrill Lynch.

Despite the shock rise in July, the trade deficit was likely to shrink in coming months, analysts said. Most of the July import increase reflected higher oil prices, which should fade, and forward-looking indicators suggest exports will improve.
The dollar lost more than a yen and was at 108.96/109.01 yen at 1435 GMT, down from 110.17/27 in late European trade on Tuesday. Against the mark, it was also lower at 1.5070/80 marks.
That compared with 1.5140/50 marks at the close here on Tuesday. Support at 1.5060/50 slowed the decline, traders said.
A large trade deficit tends to depress the dollar's value because when a country imports more than it exports, dollars flows out into the currency market to pay for those imports.
An unexpected 3.6 percent drop in exports prompted analysts to lower forecasts for third quarter growth. Many now expect a 2.0-2.5 percent rate after 4.8 percent in the second quarter.
"This deterioration in net exports may cause some downward revisions to third quarter GDP estimates," said Jeremy Hawkins, chief economic adviser at Bank America.

The dollar continued to get some support from the market's fixation on future monetary policy in the U.S., analysts said. Interest rate rise speculation was reignited on Tuesday by news most Federal Reserve Banks were lobbying for a rise in the discount rate, currently at 5.0 percent.
The Fed's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee meets on September 24.

"The interest rate support is still in place, but some sort of rate rise is clearly priced into the dollar already, which is likely to keep it within the familiar ranges for now," said Keith Edmonds, chief analyst at IBJ International.

Dealers will be eyeing comments by Fed members, scheduled to speak in the next few days, for further clues about U.S. monetary policy. Fed vice-chair Alice Rivlin speaks to the Institute of International Bankers in New York at 1715 GMT.

The French franc weakened on profi-taking after its recent surge against the mark but found strong support at 3.41.It closed at 3.4071/76 from 3.3980/83. The French budget, extensively leaked in the press, had only a marginal effect.
The Finnish markka was little changed after the Bank of Finland cut is key tender rate by 15 basis points to 3.10 percent. The markka stood at 3.0010 per mark versus 2.9975.
